You could easily sum up the back story of Chronicles of Narnia as various kids, usually family members, are magically transported to another world unlike their own where their presence causes a disruption to the events unfolding.

That's part of the reason Harry Potter was so successful though. She took a fundamental archetype and fleshed it out. Involved back stories and character development simply aren't what most kids want. They want a good guy a bad guy and a conflict. The same critique could be applied to some of the most successful SF worlds (Star Wars prior to fan involvement is a good example here) It was the right genre at the right time with the right age range. The big difference between your examples and Harry Potter is intended age range IMO. While the Chronicles of Narnia is a children's book the overt christian themes in it put it out of reach of the average reader today also children's books tend to have a shorter shelf life particularly in the tween market as kids want to read what's "cool".
I'm not saying that HP is great literature (it isn't by any stretch) but she managed to create an immersive world using tried and true archetypal characters updated for a more modern audience. By all means I don't think 20 years from now anyone will give a shit about HP but it was a good series for what it was (well the last few books kind of got away from her).
